title: Software Requirements Specification (IEEE 830) — New Requirements Chat

sections.title: 1. Technical Introduction & Purpose
sections.body:
This Software Requirements Specification (SRS) defines the formal technical and engineering requirements for **New Requirements Chat** in the **HEALTHCARE** domain.

The document provides a high-level functional overview of a Hospital Management System (HMS), listing core modules (EMR, Billing, Pharmacy, etc.) and a suggested tech stack (React, FastAPI/Node, PostgreSQL). However, it lacks the technical depth, specific compliance mappings (HIPAA/GDPR), data standards (HL7 FHIR/DICOM), and non-functional benchmarks required for a production-grade healthcare system. It reads as a generic software requirements outline rather than a rigorous architectural specification.

sections.title: 2. Overall Description & System Architecture
sections.body:
The platform is architected as an enterprise-grade service complying with HIPAA, GDPR (if EU patients), HL7 FHIR, DICOM.

It interfaces with secure API endpoints, relational persistence layers, and client-facing interfaces with strict multi-tenant boundary isolation.

sections.title: 3. Detailed Functional Requirements Specification
table: Shall implement Patient Registration and Profile Management with deterministic error handling and boundary validation.
Verify that patient data is encrypted at rest (AES-256) and that PII is masked in logs.
Shall implement Electronic Medical Records (EMR) with deterministic error handling and boundary validation.
Verify that clinical notes are stored in HL7 FHIR format and that audit logs are immutable.
Shall implement Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) with deterministic error handling and boundary validation.
Verify that a Nurse cannot access billing data and that MFA is enforced for staff login.
Shall implement Laboratory Test Requests and Reports with deterministic error handling and boundary validation.
Verify that lab results are exchanged via HL7 FHIR Observation resources and that DICOM images are supported if applicable.
Shall implement Billing and Payments with deterministic error handling and boundary validation.
Verify that payment data is PCI-DSS compliant and that PHI is not stored in payment logs.
Shall implement Audit Logs with deterministic error handling and boundary validation.
Verify that audit logs are tamper-proof and that access to logs is restricted to security administrators.

sections.title: 4. Non-Functional Requirements (NFR)
sections.body:
• **Domain Standards (HEALTHCARE)**: Enforces HIPAA, GDPR (if EU patients), HL7 FHIR, DICOM.
• **NFR-1**: PHI encryption at rest (AES-256)
• **NFR-2**: audit trail immutability
• **NFR-3**: RTO < 1h / RPO < 5min

sections.title: 5. External Interface Requirements
sections.body:
• **API Protocols**: RESTful HTTPS endpoints with JSON schema payload validation.
• **Security Layer**: OAuth2 / JWT authentication with role-based access control.
• **Data Protection**: TLS 1.3 in-transit and AES-256 at-rest per HIPAA, GDPR (if EU patients), HL7 FHIR, DICOM.

sections.title: 6. System Constraints & Compliance Verification
sections.body: System operation is bounded by HIPAA, GDPR (if EU patients), HL7 FHIR, DICOM specifications. Any unquantified requirements from the source document are tracked as open architecture items requiring stakeholder signoff.

_source_audit.summary: The document provides a high-level functional overview of a Hospital Management System (HMS), listing core modules (EMR, Billing, Pharmacy, etc.) and a suggested tech stack (React, FastAPI/Node, PostgreSQL). However, it lacks the technical depth, specific compliance mappings (HIPAA/GDPR), data standards (HL7 FHIR/DICOM), and non-functional benchmarks required for a production-grade healthcare system. It reads as a generic software requirements outline rather than a rigorous architectural specification.

risk_factors.title: Lack of Specific PHI Encryption Standards
risk_factors.description: The document mentions 'password encryption' and 'privacy of medical information' but fails to specify encryption standards for Protected Health Information (PHI) at rest or in transit. It does not mandate AES-256 for data at rest or TLS 1.2+ for data in transit, which are HIPAA Security Rule requirements.
risk_factors.mitigation: Explicitly specify AES-256 encryption for all PHI fields in the database and TLS 1.2/1.3 for all API communications. Define key management strategies (e.g., KMS) for encryption keys.

verification.claim: Risk: Lack of Specific PHI Encryption Standards — The document mentions 'password encryption' and 'privacy of medical information' but fails to specify encryption standards for Protected Health Information (PHI) at rest or in transit. It does not mandate AES-256 for data at rest or TLS 1.2+ for data in transit, which are HIPAA Security Rule requirements.
verification.reason: Source mentions password encryption and privacy but gives no PHI encryption standards.

risk_factors.title: Absence of Audit Trail Immutability
risk_factors.description: The document lists 'audit logs' as a feature but does not define the integrity or immutability of these logs. In healthcare, audit trails must be tamper-proof to satisfy HIPAA and GDPR accountability requirements.
risk_factors.mitigation: Specify that audit logs must be written to an append-only storage system or blockchain-based ledger to ensure immutability. Define retention periods and access controls for audit logs.

verification.claim: Risk: Absence of Audit Trail Immutability — The document lists 'audit logs' as a feature but does not define the integrity or immutability of these logs. In healthcare, audit trails must be tamper-proof to satisfy HIPAA and GDPR accountability requirements.
verification.reason: Audit logs are listed without any immutability or tamper‑proof guarantees.

risk_factors.title: Missing Interoperability Standards (HL7 FHIR/DICOM)
risk_factors.description: The document mentions 'electronic medical records' and 'laboratory test reports' but does not reference HL7 FHIR or DICOM standards. This creates a siloed system that cannot easily exchange data with other healthcare providers or imaging devices.
risk_factors.mitigation: Integrate HL7 FHIR R4 for clinical data exchange and DICOM for medical imaging. Define API endpoints that conform to FHIR resources (Patient, Observation, MedicationRequest).

verification.claim: Risk: Missing Interoperability Standards (HL7 FHIR/DICOM) — The document mentions 'electronic medical records' and 'laboratory test reports' but does not reference HL7 FHIR or DICOM standards. This creates a siloed system that cannot easily exchange data with other healthcare providers or imaging devices.
verification.reason: EMR and lab reports are described but HL7 FHIR or DICOM are not referenced.

risk_factors.title: Undefined Disaster Recovery Benchmarks
risk_factors.description: The document mentions 'backup/recovery' and 'high availability' but provides no specific Recovery Time Objective (RTO) or Recovery Point Objective (RPO). For a hospital system, downtime can be life-threatening.
risk_factors.mitigation: Define RTO < 1 hour and RPO < 5 minutes. Specify active-active or active-passive database replication strategies to meet these benchmarks.

verification.claim: Risk: Undefined Disaster Recovery Benchmarks — The document mentions 'backup/recovery' and 'high availability' but provides no specific Recovery Time Objective (RTO) or Recovery Point Objective (RPO). For a hospital system, downtime can be life-threatening.
verification.reason: Backup/recovery and high availability are mentioned without RTO/RPO metrics.

risk_factors.title: Ambiguous Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) Granularity
risk_factors.description: The document lists roles (Admin, Doctor, Nurse, etc.) but does not specify the granularity of access. For example, it is unclear if a Nurse can view financial billing data or if a Doctor can modify another Doctor's clinical notes.
risk_factors.mitigation: Define a detailed RBAC matrix mapping each role to specific CRUD permissions for each data entity (e.g., Patient, Invoice, Prescription). Implement least-privilege principles.

verification.claim: Risk: Ambiguous Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) Granularity — The document lists roles (Admin, Doctor, Nurse, etc.) but does not specify the granularity of access. For example, it is unclear if a Nurse can view financial billing data or if a Doctor can modify another Doctor's clinical notes.
verification.reason: Roles are enumerated but no detail on access granularity for each role.

conflicts_and_ambiguities.context: The document states 'secure authentication, password encryption, session management, HTTPS' but does not specify multi-factor authentication (MFA) or specific password complexity policies.
conflicts_and_ambiguities.suggested_resolution: Mandate MFA for all staff roles. Specify password complexity rules (e.g., NIST 800-63B) and session timeout durations (e.g., 15 minutes of inactivity).

verification.claim: Ambiguity: Vague Definition of 'Secure Authentication' — The document states 'secure authentication, password encryption, session management, HTTPS' but does not specify multi-factor authentication (MFA) or specific password complexity policies.
verification.reason: Secure authentication is noted without MFA or detailed password policies.

conflicts_and_ambiguities.issue: Unclear Data Ownership and Consent Management
conflicts_and_ambiguities.context: The document mentions 'patient registration' and 'privacy of medical information' but does not address patient consent for data sharing or GDPR rights (right to erasure, portability).
conflicts_and_ambiguities.suggested_resolution: Implement a consent management module that tracks patient consent for data usage. Define workflows for handling GDPR data subject access requests (DSAR) and right to be forgotten.

verification.claim: Ambiguity: Unclear Data Ownership and Consent Management — The document mentions 'patient registration' and 'privacy of medical information' but does not address patient consent for data sharing or GDPR rights (right to erasure, portability).
verification.reason: Privacy is referenced but patient consent and data ownership are omitted.

conflicts_and_ambiguities.context: The document lists 'fast API responses' as a non-functional requirement but provides no measurable latency targets.
conflicts_and_ambiguities.suggested_resolution: Define specific latency benchmarks, e.g., 95th percentile API response time < 200ms for read operations and < 500ms for write operations.

verification.claim: Ambiguity: Ambiguous 'Fast API Responses' Benchmark — The document lists 'fast API responses' as a non-functional requirement but provides no measurable latency targets.
verification.reason: Fast API responses are required but no latency targets are provided.

missing_sections_and_details.recommended_addition: Add a section detailing how each technical control (encryption, access control, audit logs) maps to specific HIPAA Security Rule standards (45 CFR 164.312).

verification.reason: Only generic backup/recovery is noted; no detailed DR/BC plan is included.

missing_sections_and_details.why_missing: No threat model is provided to identify potential attack vectors (e.g., SQL injection, XSS, privilege escalation) specific to the HMS.

Implement AES-256 encryption for all PHI at rest and TLS 1.2+ for data in transit, with a dedicated Key Management Service (KMS) for key rotation and access control.
Define and enforce immutable audit trails using append-only storage or blockchain technology to satisfy HIPAA and GDPR accountability requirements.
Specify concrete RTO (< 1 hour) and RPO (< 5 minutes) benchmarks for disaster recovery and implement active-active database replication to meet these targets.
Develop a detailed RBAC matrix that maps each role to specific CRUD permissions for each data entity, ensuring least-privilege access and preventing unauthorized data exposure.

_doc_excerpt:
File: A Hospital Management System.pdf
--- Page 1 ---
Hospital Management System 
A Hospital Management System (HMS)  should provide a centralized platform for 
managing hospital operations, patient information, medical records, appointments, doctors, 
nurses, staff, billing, pharmacy, laboratory, and inventory. The system should support  role-
based access  for Admin, Doctor, Nurse, Receptionist, Pharmacist, Lab Technician, 
Accountant, and Patient. Core requirements should include patient registration and profile 
management, appointment scheduling and queue management, doctor availability, O PD/IPD 
management, admission/discharge/transfer, electronic medical records, diagnosis, 
prescriptions, treatment history, allergies, vital signs, nursing notes, laboratory test requests 
and reports, pharmacy prescriptions and medicine inventory, bed/ward m anagement, billing 
and payments, insurance management, invoices and receipts, hospital expenses, staff 
management, and inventory/procurement. Patients should be able to view appointments, 
prescriptions, reports, bills, and medical history through a portal,  while doctors should have 
dashboards for appointments, patient records, diagnosis, prescriptions, and clinical notes. 
The system should also provide  dashboards, notifications, search/filtering, reports, audit 
logs, data validation, backup/recovery, security, and role -based authorization . 
Functional requirements should cover complete workflows such as  patient registration → 
appointment → consultation → diagnosis → laboratory/pharmacy → billing → follow -
up, and admission → bed allocation → treatment → investigations → discharge → final 
billing. Non -functional requirements should include responsive web UI, scalability, high 
availability, fast API responses , secure authentication, password encryption, session 
management, HTTPS, database integrity, auditability, privacy of medical information, error 
handling, logging, and regular backups. A suitable architecture can use  React/Next.js for 
frontend, FastAPI/Node.js/Spring Boot for backend, PostgreSQL/MySQL for database, 
REST APIs, JWT/OAuth-based authentication, Redis for caching/queues, and cloud or 
on-premise deployment , with separate modules for  Authentication, Patients, 
Appointments, EMR, Doctors, Nursing, L aboratory, Pharmacy, Billing, Inventory, 
Staff, Reports, Notifications, and Administration.
